Content:
Not every square matrix is diagonalizable. However, if a square matrix is not diagonalizable, it is "almost" diagonalizable.

Content:
More precisely, every [MATH: n\times n] matrix [MATH: A] can be written in the form

Content:
[MATH: A = PJP^{-1},]

Content:
where [MATH: J] is a Jordan matrix, and [MATH: P] is an invertible matrix. We say that [MATH: J] is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of [MATH: A.]

Content:
Not all square matrices have corresponding diagonal matrices. However, all square matrices have Jordan canonical forms. A Jordan canonical form is either diagonal or "almost" diagonal.

Content:
Our goal in this lesson is to find a Jordan canonical form of any [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix.

Content:
If a matrix is diagonalizable, then finding its Jordan canonical form is equivalent to finding its diagonal form.

Content:
For diagonalizable [MATH: 2\times 2] matrices, we have two separate cases:

Content:
- [MATH: A] has two distinct eigenvalues.
- [MATH: A] is a scalar matrix. A diagonal matrix is scalar if every value on the leading diagonal is the same.

Content:
Let's discuss these two cases first. Then, we will discuss the final case, which is when [MATH: A] is not diagonalizable.

sections.normalized_html:
Every [MATH: n\times n] matrix [MATH: A] can be written in the form [MATH: A = PJP^{-1},] where [MATH: J] is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of [MATH: A,] and [MATH: P] is an invertible matrix.

To find the matrix [MATH: J,] we first find the eigenvalues of the matrix [MATH: A] by solving [MATH: \det(A-\lambda I)=0{:}]

[MATH: |5 − λ|4; 2|− 2 − λ||= 0; (5 − λ)(− 2 − λ) − 4 ⋅ 2|= 0; λ^{2} − 3λ − 18|= 0; (λ − 6)(λ + 3)|= 0]

So, the eigenvalues are [MATH: \lambda_1=-3] and [MATH: \lambda_2=6.] Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix [MATH: A] is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

[MATH: [− 3|0; 0|6]]

Note: A Jordan canonical form is unique up to permutations of its Jordan blocks. Therefore, another Jordan canonical form for this matrix is

[MATH: [6|0; 0|− 3]]

Content:

Item 1 — Tutorial: Introduction

[MATH: A = PJP^{-1},]

Content:
where [MATH: J] is a Jordan matrix, and [MATH: P] is an invertible matrix. We say that [MATH: J] is a Jordan canonical form (or Jordan normal form) of [MATH: A.]

Content:
Not all square matrices have corresponding diagonal matrices. However, all square matrices have Jordan canonical forms. A Jordan canonical form is either diagonal or "almost" diagonal.

Content:
Our goal in this lesson is to find a Jordan canonical form of any [MATH: 2\times 2] matrix.

[MATH: A = PJP^{-1},]

So, the eigenvalues are [MATH: \lambda_1=-3] and [MATH: \lambda_2=6.] Since we get two distinct eigenvalues, the matrix [MATH: A] is diagonalizable, and a Jordan canonical form is

[MATH: [− 3|0; 0|6]]

Item 12 — Tutorial: Overview of All Possible Jordan Canonical Forms of 2x2 Matrices

Content:
Given a [MATH: 2 \times 2] matrix [MATH: A,] we have [MATH: 3] possible cases:

Content:
- If [MATH: A] has two distinct eigenvalues [MATH: \lambda_1 \neq \lambda_2,] then [MATH: A] is diagonalizable, and [MATH: J] is a diagonal matrix. In this case, [MATH: J] is a composition of two distinct [MATH: 1 \times 1] Jordan blocks:
[MATH: [λ_{1}|0; 0|λ_{2}]]
- If [MATH: A] has only one eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda] of algebraic multiplicity [MATH: 2] and there exist two linearly independent eigenvectors corresponding to this eigenvalue, then [MATH: A] must be a scalar matrix. This situation corresponds to the case where [MATH: A] is already diagonalized, and [MATH: J] is a composition of two identical [MATH: 1 \times 1] Jordan blocks:
[MATH: [λ|0; 0|λ]]
- If [MATH: A] has only one eigenvalue [MATH: \lambda] of algebraic multiplicity [MATH: 2] and only one linearly independent eigenvector exists that corresponds to this eigenvalue, then [MATH: A] is not diagonalizable. In this case, [MATH: J] is a single [MATH: 2 \times 2] Jordan block:
[MATH: [λ|1; 0|λ]]

Content:
So, in two out of three cases, our matrix is diagonalizable. But in the third case, the closest we can get to a diagonal matrix is a Jordan block with a [MATH: 1] on the superdiagonal.
